title: Scaling Node.js Applications
learning_outcomes: Describe Vertical and horizontal scaling and explain how it relates to Scaling Node.js Applications.
Demonstrate Stateless service design in a small Node.js example and predict the observable result.
Test a failure, boundary, lifecycle, or version-compatibility case involving Shared external state.

content.intro: Scaling Node.js Applications is part of architecture and production grade systems. This lesson connects Vertical and horizontal scaling, Stateless service design, Shared external state to a concrete Node.js example. Focus on the behavior you can observe, the assumptions the API makes, and one failure or boundary case.
content.why_it_matters: Production architecture balances module boundaries, consistency, failure isolation, latency, operational complexity, and team needs. Trace a request through services and storage, then test retry, partial failure, duplicate delivery, and recovery behavior.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: Production architecture balances module boundaries, consistency, failure isolation, latency, operational complexity, and team needs. Make trade-offs explicit, design idempotent boundaries, and add service separation only when it solves a demonstrated need.

content_blocks.title: Runtime and safety note
content_blocks.text: Teaching baseline: use a supported Node.js LTS release (Node.js 24 LTS as checked on 2026-10-13). The official releases page lists Node.js 26 as Current and Node.js 24/22 as LTS. Some advanced APIs, flags, permission behavior, embedded SQLite capabilities, module-loader hooks, and TypeScript integration are version-sensitive; verify the exact installed runtime. The Node.js 22 runtime available in the build-check environment is used only for syntax checks. This example is for learning and static validation, not for executing untrusted learner code inside CodeLeaf.

content.task: Create or inspect a small Node.js example for Scaling Node.js Applications. Include at least one listed subtopic, document the expected result, and verify a normal case plus a boundary or failure case.
task_acceptance_criteria: The example demonstrates a named lesson concept, rather than only mentioning the title.
Expected output or observable behavior is documented and reproducible.
At least one invalid, empty, timeout, resource, or failure case is handled or explained.
The solution does not put secrets in source code and does not execute untrusted code inside the production API process.
hints: Start with Vertical and horizontal scaling; identify the input, operation, and observable result.
Run the smallest relevant example in the selected Node.js release before adding frameworks or external services.
Test one failure or boundary case for Stateless service design, then explain why the outcome is expected.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming microservices, queues, or multiple worker processes automatically make a system more reliable.
common_mistakes.why: The code may pass a simple demonstration yet fail with real inputs, resource limits, timing, or runtime differences.
common_mistakes.fix: Start with clear boundaries and measurable requirements, then document the operational cost of each architecture choice.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying a snippet without checking its runtime, dependencies, input assumptions, or cleanup behavior.
common_mistakes.why: Node.js APIs and surrounding ecosystem tools have explicit version, trust, and resource boundaries.
common_mistakes.fix: State the environment and dependency assumptions, then rerun the example from a clean starting state.
